ACT-J01
PASSAGE IV
A Basic Bike Ride
In June of 1972, two young married couples, the
Siples and the Burdens, left Anchorage, Alaska, on
bicycles laden with camping gear and food. Their goal
was simple but ambitious: to cycle the length of North
and South America on a one-way, hemisphere-spanning
trip dubbed “Hemistour.” Unfortunately, on the first
night, as the cyclists lay sleeping, somebody stole
many of their supplies.
The riders reacted to this setback with a resilience
that would serve them well: they just kept pedaling.
This can-do attitude was key to their aim of publicizing,
both to the people they met and through the media, that
bicycle expeditions—almost unheard-of at the time—was
an engaging, inexpensive way to travel. Also, the cyclists
wanted to show that everyday people could make such a
trip—the riders were not professional athletes.
] Hemistour was rarely, however, easy. [
] Inching
across Alaska on thirty-pound bicycles bearing fifty
pounds of supplies apiece, the Siples and Burdens
dealt with clouds of mosquitoes and too many bumpy
gravel roads. [
] In Canada, they faced slopes too steep

tion (adjusting the punctuation as needed). Should the

F.
Kept, because it helps explain why the riders did
not give up after losing many of their supplies.
G.
Kept, because it portrays the riders’ actions and
helps express their resilience.
H.
Deleted, because it interrupts the explanation of
the riders’ goals and characterizes their attitudes
as unsophisticated.
J.
Deleted, because it doesn’t explain how the riders
managed to continue without all their supplies.
